title: Hamel Family Wines Makes a Statement in Sonoma
summary:
Sample Bordeaux-style wines shaped by volcanic soils at a sleek, modern winery in Sonoma.

The post Hamel Family Wines Makes a Statement in Sonoma appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Winemakers often gush about grapes grown in volcanic soils, but what does that mean in the glass? Rich in minerals, these porous soils allow roots to dig deep for water and nutrients — resulting in smaller, more concentrated berries prized for their intensity and mineral notes. At scenic Hamel Family Wines in Sonoma, visitors can taste those distinctions.

The story

George Hamel Jr., the co-founder of a San Francisco-based investment management firm, got his first taste of Wine Country life in 2006, when he and his wife, Pamela, bought a house in Kenwood and started growing an acre of Cabernet Sauvignon on the site — later dubbed Tres Palma Vineyard.

Four years later, they acquired 120 acres of land in Sonoma Valley and developed the Hamel Estate Vineyard. The couple then added Nuns Canyon Vineyard in Moon Mountain, planted on a volcanic property along the steep slopes of the Mayacamas Mountains, and opened Hamel Family Winery in 2014.

John Hamel, George and Pamela’s son, now heads up winemaking and viticulture, crafting estate-grown wines from the family’s certified organic and biodynamic vineyards. The winery farms a total of 91 acres of dry-farmed Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Grenache and Sauvignon Blanc.

The vibe

Designed by celebrated architect Douglas Thornley of Gould Evans, the sleek, modern winery makes a statement with 18-foot-high windows and an expansive terrace that showcases Hamel’s estate vineyards and Sonoma Mountain views.

Whether seated inside or on the patio, you’ll feel immersed in the beautiful landscape. Extending into a hillside behind the winery is an immaculate 12,000-square-foot wine cave used for barrel and cask storage. An exposed section of the cave wall reveals layers of volcanic soils that shape Hamel’s wines.

On the palate

Hamel began moving toward a new winemaking style in 2020, focusing on minerality and freshness. To put volcanic terroir front and center, the winery uses neutral aging vessels such as large oak casks, concrete tanks and clay vessels.

The 2024 Nuns Canyon Sauvignon Blanc from Moon Mountain ($80) is crisp and balanced, showing bright citrus flavors and brisk acidity. The 2020 Isthmus Cabernet Sauvignon ($90) is a gently structured, elegant wine with aromas of black fruits and flavors of ripe blackberries.

I was wowed by the 2023 Nuns Canyon Grenache ($110), with its bouquet of red berries, cherries, savory notes and spice. The wine expertly combines freshness with complexity.

Tastings range from $95 for a tour and tasting of current releases paired with a seasonal snack to $200 for the Chef’s Experience, a communal tasting combining library wines and current releases, matched with exquisite small plates such as Liberty Farms duck breast and ricotta gnocchi with huckleberries.

Beyond the bottle

As much as I love a high-end food pairing experience, I frequently have a hankering for more down-to-earth eats.

Next-level smashburgers from the team behind Glen Ellen Star and Stella are a short drive away at Smash. The fast-casual eatery on Sonoma Plaza serves crispy-edged beef patties, plus fried chicken sandos and shakes.

If you’d prefer to enjoy your burgers in a more adult setting, take them upstairs to the Beacon speakeasy.

The details: Hamel Family Wines is open by appointment daily. 15401 Sonoma Highway, Sonoma. 707-996-5800, hamelfamilywines.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma magazine. Follow Tina on Instagram @winebroad and view her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: Where To Find Pumpkin Spice Lattes and Sweet Treats in Sonoma County
summary:
Crafty Sonoma County bakers and baristas are offering up a wide assortment of creative, pumpkin-infused drinks and treats this season.

The post Where To Find Pumpkin Spice Lattes and Sweet Treats in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Whether “pumpkin spice season” inspires autumnal bliss or exasperated groans, it’s hard to deny the appeal of fall’s comforting flavors: cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger and, of course, pumpkin.

Across Sonoma County, bakers, baristas and ice cream makers are embracing the season with an abundance of pumpkin-infused drinks and treats, from the familiar pumpkin spice latte to pumpkin scones, cheesecakes, pies and ice cream.

Here are more than 40 places to find pumpkin spice drinks and dishes this fall.

Santa Rosa

Blondie’s Bakery Boutique

The downtown bakery has a pumpkin pie cupcake filled with pumpkin mousse and topped with cream cheese frosting and toasted pumpkin crumble. 404 Mendocino Ave., Suite A, Santa Rosa, 707-843-7335, blondiesbakeryboutique.com

Brew Coffee and Beer House

The cozy cafe has brought back its seasonal pumpkin spice latte, made with housemade pumpkin spice syrup and topped with festive latte art. Also available: pumpkin chai and cold brew with pumpkin cold foam. 555 Healdsburg Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-303-7372, brewcoffeeandbeer.com

Café de la Olla

This small Roseland coffee kiosk recently featured a pumpkin-peanut butter latte. Pumpkin cold foam can also be added to lattes. Check Instagram, @cafe_de_la_olla, for new creative pumpkin drink drops. 959 Sebastopol Road, Santa Rosa, 510-695-1875, cafe-de-la-olla-llc.square.site

Criminal Baking Company

The bakery is offering a pumpkin cake with roasted apples and caramel filling, finished with vanilla buttercream. It is available in multiple sizes. 808 Donahue St., Santa Rosa, 707-888-3546, criminalbakingcompany.com

Crooks Coffee

It’s fitting that this Edgar Allan Poe-themed coffee shop leans into the spooky season with fall drinks. While its autumn menu has yet to be released, past offerings have included the classic pumpkin spice latte, white pumpkin pie latte and cold brew with pumpkin spice foam, along with pumpkin bread and pumpkin pie scones. 404 Mendocino Ave., Suite C, Santa Rosa, 707-791-3365, crookscoffeehouse.com

Dave’s Gourmet Ice Cream

The fall menu includes pumpkin chocolate chip and pumpkin swirl cheesecake ice creams. 320 W. Third St., Suite D, Santa Rosa, 707-978-2635, dgicecream.com

Johnny Doughnuts

The local doughnut shop has brought back its pumpkin brown butter cake doughnut, a fluffy, spiced pumpkin cake topped with a brown butter glaze. It’s a perfect coffee companion for chilly fall mornings. There’s also a pumpkin latte. 1200 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-308-4836, johnnydoughnuts.com

Land and Water Coffee

Seasonal drinks include pumpkin spice and pumpkin chai lattes. 1301 Cleveland Ave., Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-527-3725; 621 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-527-3731, landandwater.coffee

Salt & Straw

The Portland-based ice cream chain, which opened a Santa Rosa location last year, is offering Jack o’ Lantern Pumpkin Bread ice cream as part of its rotating monthly menu. The Halloween-inspired flavor combines pumpkin spice ice cream with pieces of chewy pumpkin bread and cream cheese frosting. 700 Village Court, Santa Rosa, 707-360-6249, saltandstraw.com

Wooden Petal Pretzel Parlor

The shop recently featured pumpkin cinnamon rolls on its Saturday secret menu, available from 8 a.m. to noon. Check Instagram, @woodenpetal.pretzelparlor, for future specials. 4984 Sonoma Highway, Santa Rosa, 707-695-1880, woodenpetal.com

Petaluma

The Bagel Mill

This Petaluma bagel shop offers pumpkin spice lattes, chais and white mochas made with housemade pumpkin spice puree from local organic sugar pie pumpkins. Its seasonal pumpkin spice cream cheese is back, too. 212 Western Ave., Petaluma, 707-981-8010, thebagelmill.com

Caffeine Inc.

The Petaluma coffee shop offers a pumpkin pie latte, which includes pumpkin puree, pumpkin spice syrup, maple and espresso. 775 Baywood Drive, Petaluma, 707-774-6016, caffeineinc.net

Petaluma Brunch Station

Pumpkin pancakes are on the menu at this all-day brunch spot. Make them a combo with two eggs cooked to order and bacon or sausage. 732 E. Washington St., Petaluma, 707-762-4095, thebrunchstation.com

Petaluma Coffee & Tea

At this longtime Petaluma coffeehouse, customers can add pumpkin pie syrup to any coffee, latte, mocha, chai or cappuccino for $1. 212 Second St., Petaluma, 707-763-2727, petalumacoffee.com

Petaluma Pie Company

The bakery puts a twist on the traditional pumpkin pie with a maple pumpkin version made with organic pumpkin, vanilla, cinnamon, cloves, ginger, brown sugar and maple syrup. 125 Petaluma Blvd. N., Suite B, Petaluma, 707-766-6743, petalumapiecompany.com

Pink Owl Coffee

The cafe’s pumpkin spice latte is flavored with pumpkin syrup and “a hint of pumpkin pie dust.” Pumpkin spice syrup can also be added to most drinks. 617 E. Washington St., Petaluma, 707-658-2274, pinkowlcoffee.com

Stellina Pronto

This Italian bakery and cafe keeps a New York-style pumpkin cheesecake on its regular menu. Seasonal offerings have included pumpkin ricotta tarts. 23 Kentucky St., Petaluma, 707-789-9556, stellinapronto.com

Penngrove

Odd Cookie Bakery

This quirky bakery got an early start on pumpkin season, introducing pumpkin cookies, cupcakes and a pumpkin cake cup layered with New York-style cheesecake, graham cracker crust and whipped cream in August. September brought another version made with espresso tres leches, espresso pudding and whipped cream. Check Instagram, @oddcookiebakery, for new pumpkin treats. 10000 Main St., Penngrove, 707-283-7772, oddcookiebakery.com

Cotati

Cotati Coffee Company

Customers can add housemade pumpkin spice syrup to any drink for 75 cents. The syrup also appears in fall specials such as the Scarecrow Latte, made with maple, hazelnut, honey and cinnamon. 8225 Old Redwood Highway, Cotati, 707-992-0005, cotati-coffee-company.square.site

Rohnert Park

Squatch’s Gourmet Ice Cream Sandwiches and Coffee

The cafe and ice cream shop is offering a pumpkin cheesecake ice cream sandwich, or “Squatch,” made with snickerdoodle cookies and graham crackers. The Halloween-themed “Spooky Squatch,” pairs pumpkin cheesecake ice cream with chocolate-chocolate chip cookies and Halloween sprinkles. Other seasonal offerings include a pumpkin spice latte, pumpkin cream cold brew, iced pumpkin cream chai and pumpkin affogato. 1451 Southwest Blvd., Suite 111, Rohnert Park, 707-992-0841, squatchscoffee.com

Sebastopol

Muir’s Tea Room

Muir’s annual Black Hat Society High Tea, offered Oct. 3 through Oct. 31, features a Harvest Moon Pumpkin Scone served with housemade lemon curd, clotted “cream” and imported English preserves. Pumpkin scones are also available a la carte, along with pumpkin spice chocolate chip cookies. 330 S. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-634-6143, muirstearoomandcafe.com

Patisserie Angelica

The Parisian-style bakery offers pumpkin pie, pumpkin scones, pumpkin muffins, spiced pumpkin cheesecake and an autumn-themed pumpkin cake. 6821 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol, 707-827-7998, patisserieangelica.com

Retrograde Coffee Roasters

The pumpkin spice latte is made with real pumpkin puree. There’s also a pumpkin spice cold brew sweetened with housemade vanilla syrup and topped with pumpkin spice cold foam. Bottles of pumpkin spice puree are available for purchase. 130 S. Main St., Suite 103, Sebastopol, 707-969-7234, retrograderoasters.com

Screamin’ Mimi’s Ice Cream

Come October, Screamin’ Mimi’s offers its seasonal special pumpkin mud pie ice cream, a seasonal riff on the popular chocolate Mimi’s Mud, with pumpkin replacing the espresso. 6902 Sebastopol Ave., Sebastopol, 707-823-5902, screaminmimisicecream.com

Society Bakery and Cafe

The cafe offers pumpkin spice and pumpkin chai lattes made with fall spices and housemade pumpkin syrup, along with a pumpkin white chocolate mocha and pumpkin sweet cream matcha. Seasonal baked goods include pumpkin maple cake, pumpkin cinnamon rolls, pumpkin chocolate chip cookies and pumpkin-pecan upside-down cake. Nine-inch pumpkin cheesecakes are available in November and December. 2661 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol, 707-861-9665, societybakerycafe.com

Taylor Lane Organic Coffee

The Barlow cafe offers pumpkin spice lattes in the fall, along with seasonal pumpkin pecan scones. 6790 McKinley St., Suite 170, Sebastopol, 707-634-7129, taylorlane.com

Two Dog Night Creamery

The creamery changes its ice cream flavors with the seasons. In October, be sure to look for organic pumpkin ice cream; pumpkin pie ice cream follows in November. 6760 McKinley St., Suite 110, Sebastopol, 707-823-9376, twodognightcreamery.com

Windsor

Grey Squirrel Manor

The cafe serves a pumpkin spice latte made with Land and Water coffee and fall spices. 630 McClelland Drive, Windsor, 707-243-3551, greysquirrelmanor.com

Healdsburg

Black Oak Coffee Roasters

The fall menu includes the shop’s popular housemade pumpkin latte, made with scratch-made pumpkin sauce and fall spices. 324 Center St., Healdsburg, 866-390-1427, blackoakcoffee.com

Costeaux French Bakery

The bakery offers a classic pumpkin pie and a seasonal pumpkin latte made with Monin Pumpkin Pie Syrup. 417 Healdsburg Ave., Healdsburg, 707-433-1913, costeaux.com

Little Saint

The vegan restaurant currently features a pumpkin creme brulee, which includes a cream cheese mousse and ginger cookie crumble. 25 North St., Healdsburg, 707-433-8207, littlesainthealdsburg.com

The Taste of Tea

The Japanese tea and ramen shop offers a pumpkin pie latte and pumpkin spice boba made with black tea, oat milk, pumpkin spice syrup and tapioca pearls. 109 North St., Healdsburg, 707-431-1995, thetasteoftea.com

Kenwood

Pillowfight Coffee

Named for Kenwood’s historic World Pillow Fighting Championship, this cafe serves locally sourced coffee, teas and matchas. Its housemade pumpkin spice syrup goes into the pumpkin spice latte, pumpkin cold brew and pumpkin chai. 8910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B12, Kenwood, pillowfight.coffee

Sonoma

Darling, an Ice Cream Shop

This shop rotates its ice cream flavors monthly. Its September menu includes pumpkin brandy ice cream made with brandy from Prohibition Spirits. The October menu is scheduled for release on Oct. 7. 201 W. Napa St., Suite 6, Sonoma, 707-343-1482, darlingsonoma.com

Smastad Coffee Roasters

This Swedish-inspired cafe’s fall specials include a pumpkin pie latte and pumpkin coffee cake. 981 Broadway, Sonoma, 707-939-1906, smastadcoffee.com

Sunflower Caffé

The cafe’s menu features a pumpkin bread mini loaf served with whipped espresso butter, as well as pumpkin spice lattes. 421 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-6645, sonomasunflower.com

Sonoma Coast

Nom Nom Cakes

The Bodega Bay home bakery’s fall menu includes traditional pumpkin pie, pumpkin cheesecake with brown sugar praline sauce, spiced pumpkin bread and pumpkin cake with maple cream cheese buttercream. Orders are available for delivery or pickup in Bodega Bay. 390 Calle Del Sol, Bodega Bay, 805-350-0680, nomnombaking.com

Wild Flour Bread

The Freestone bakery offers spiced pumpkin bread studded with walnuts, cranberries and candied ginger — a combination that falls somewhere between pumpkin pie and gingerbread. 140 Bohemian Highway., Freestone, 707-874-2938, wildflourbread.com

Multiple locations

Acme Burger

The local burger chain is offering a pumpkin pie milkshake made with Straus organic soft serve. Locations in Cotati, Petaluma and Santa Rosa. acmeburgerco.com

Avid Coffee

The local coffee chain offers a pumpkin latte made with Sonoma Syrup Co. pumpkin pie syrup and topped with cinnamon. Pumpkin syrup can also be added to drinks including chai, mochas and cold brews. Pair a drink with the gluten-free pumpkin muffin. 21 Fourth St., Petaluma, 707-772-5117; 2365 Midway Drive, Santa Rosa, 707-595-5984, avidcoffee.com

Crumbl

The Utah-based cookie chain, with locations in Petaluma and Santa Rosa, is offering a pumpkin square made with brown sugar-cinnamon butter, vanilla cream cheese frosting and warm spices. 179 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma, 707-238-2351; 2154 Santa Rosa Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-324-1781, crumblcookies.com

Noble Folk Ice Cream & Pie Bar

The local pie and ice cream shop regularly features a classic maple pumpkin pie on its fall menu and a pumpkin chocolate cheesecake on its winter menu. The cheesecake comes in an Oreo crust, topped with chocolate ganache and cinnamon. A pumpkin chocolate ice cream is also part of the fall lineup. 539 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-978-3392; 116 Matheson St., Healdsburg, 707-395-4426, thenoblefolk.com

Plank Coffee

The north county coffee shop’s seasonal pumpkin spice latte is made with organic pumpkin, cinnamon, cloves, ginger and nutmeg, along with a double shot of house-roasted Pine Mountain Espresso. There’s also a pumpkin maple scone. 175 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg, 707-395-0572; 227 N. Cloverdale Blvd., Cloverdale, 707-894-6187, plankcoffee.com

Sunshine Coffee Roasters

The west county coffee roasters has added various pumpkin drinks and treats to its fall menu, such as pumpkin spice lattes and pumpkin cold foam chai. 6656 Front St., Forestville, 707-887-1632; 1691 Highway 116 N. and 550 Gravenstein Highway N. in Sebastopol, sunshinecoffeeroasters.com

Sweet Hartz Hand Crafted Cheesecakes

Steve Hartz, who supplies his cheesecakes to local businesses including Nightingale Breads in Forestville and Guiso Latin Fusion in Healdsburg, is making pumpkin muffins and pumpkin coffee cake this fall. His pumpkin cheesecakes may also turn up at local restaurants. For ordering information, contact Hartz at 707-321-9320 or stevehrtz@gmail.com.

The Soda Society

Sonoma County’s first dirty soda shop has a lineup of creative drinks on its fall menu, including the Headless Horseman made with Coke, pumpkin pie, pumpkin spice creamer and brown sugar cinnamon, topped with pumpkin spice whipped cream and pumpkin candies. Find the schedule on its Instagram, @the_soda_society.

title: Wildly Creative Drinks in Sonoma County To Have You Sipping Pretty
summary:
Sonoma County cafes and pop-ups are creating alluringly pretty drinks to ensure every sip through your lips is totally on trend.

The post Wildly Creative Drinks in Sonoma County To Have You Sipping Pretty appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Blame it on #DrinkTok. A wave of family-friendly, drinkable desserts is cresting as viral fruit matchas, dirty sodas and cold-foam-topped everything make their way into every corner of Sonoma County.

Peep these picks to ensure every sip through your lips is totally on trend.

Most Dirty

Alien Invasion, The Soda Society

The viral Utah sensation known as dirty soda has landed in Sonoma County, and this technicolor 24-ounce mix of Mountain Dew, blue raspberry syrup, strawberry cold foam and tart candy wants you to take it to your leader. Find The Soda Society at an event near you. instagram.com/the_soda_society

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by The Soda Society//Dirty Sodas (@the_soda_society)

Most Adorable

Raspberry Mocha Truffle, Café Carrusel

This pink-on-pink-on-pink bruncheria in downtown Santa Rosa is a pretty princess fever dream with glitter-bomb drinks like the iced mocha topped with raspberry (or banana) cold foam, edible butterflies and dried flower petals. Ridiculous, in the most delightful way. 630 Third St., Santa Rosa. 707-655-8365, instagram.com/cafe_carrusel

Most Motivating

Viet Coffee with Egg Foam, BoCo

Supercharge your Saturday farmers market run at Luther Burbank Center for the Arts with this combo of strong Vietnamese iced coffee and creamy egg foam inspired by cà phê trung. You’ll know the BoCo stand by its long line of superfans, but it’s worth the wait. They also offer home pickup in Rohnert Park. instagram.com/drink_boco

Most Nostalgic

Berry Quik Fix, SoCo Dough Co.

A liquid siren call for strawberry-milk fans who snuck a little extra pink powder into their morning moo juice. This triple threat boasts strawberry puree, strawberry milk, and strawberry whipped cream (plus a little strawberry dust on top), for a super-sweet, super-nostalgic ode to the Nesquik Bunny. Inside Graton Resort & Casino. 288 Golf Course Drive W., Rohnert Park. graton.com/fast-casual

Related: Graton Resort’s New SoCo Dough Co. Just Debuted a $275 Gold-Leaf Doughnut
Most Matcha-fied

Strawberry Shortcake Latte, Grey Squirrel Manor

This layered latte starts with strawberry jam and vanilla bean syrup, then gets a creamy middle of milk, topped by matcha tea, a float of vanilla foam and strawberry dust. Say less. 630 McClelland Drive, Windsor. 707-243-3551, greysquirrelmanor.com

Most Colorful

Butterfly Pea Lemonade, Bubbles Boba and Gifts

Dried butterfly pea flowers transform plain water into a dazzling indigo, but add citrus — lemonade works beautifully — and it blooms into magenta, purple, and pink like pure magic. Kid-safe, adult-approved, and almost too pretty to drink. Almost. 954 Gravenstein Highway S., Sebastopol. 707-861-9414, bubblesbobatea.com

title: Sonoma County Farms Helped Restaurants Reach Michelin Stars
summary:
For two restaurants newly launched into the Michelin Guide stratosphere, their journey to the stars is rooted in the earth at these Sonoma County farms.

The post Sonoma County Farms Helped Restaurants Reach Michelin Stars appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Tasting their way through the garden on a bright summer morning, chef Brian Limoges and farmer Colby Eierman have a story for nearly every ripening plant and flowering bush. In between popping kumquats in their mouths and crunching on peppers and tiny tomatoes, Limoges points out a few summer squash stalks he tried to repurpose as straws. Eierman is still surprised that a patch of near-dead gooseberries somehow came back this season. As they wind their way through the garden paths, they come across an oozing Itachi cucumber that looks like it’s been topped off with glistening rock candy or Maldon salt flakes — nature’s version of molecular gastronomy.

“Look at those juicy crystals,” says Limoges. It’s a reaction that occurs when the cucumber gets scraped, explains Eierman, before dabbing the crystalline goo with his finger and licking it like a kid polishing off leftover cake frosting. “It tastes like cucumber juice,” he says. Limoges is struck by an idea: “What if we did cucumber caviar? I don’t know if that’s practical,” he says. “Colby and I might disagree on that one.”

“I’m down,” says Eierman, not missing a beat. He laughs, but you can tell it’s hardly the craziest culinary pipe dream he’s heard over the years. Their symbiotic relationship, from the sun-drenched fields to the fast-paced kitchen, is at the core of Enclos, where multi-sensory attention to detail is elevated to an art form and one of the main reasons the Sonoma restaurant received three Michelin stars, the restaurant industry’s highest honor, in June.

Long before any emulsion is made or flames lick a saucepan on the kitchen stove, behind nearly every Michelin-starred restaurant is at least one world-class farm, if not a dozen. In fact, the anonymous Michelin inspectors who award the stars take into account ingredient quality first and foremost. In Healdsburg, reigning three-starred SingleThread grows most of its own produce. Tucker Taylor, director of culinary gardens at Jackson Family Wines, grows prized fruit and vegetables for multiple Michelin-starred restaurants around the Bay Area. Middleton Farm helped propel Healdsburg’s Troubadour to its first Michelin star this summer, too.

This harvest season, a rarefied light shines on Stone Edge Farm in Sonoma and Tierra Vegetables in Santa Rosa, two Sonoma County farms that both played an important role in catapulting Enclos and San Francisco’s Californios to the elite Michelin three-star circle for the first time.

“People have been asking, ‘What makes you special?’” says Californios chef-owner Val Cantú, who opened his restaurant in San Francisco’s Mission District in 2015. “I always say the farms and the ingredients that we get to work with here are what make us special. Everything Tierra grows is so flavorful and so delicious. We’re fortunate to be able to share their vegetables.”

He’s talking about Lee and Wayne James, salt-of-the-earth tillers of rich soil at Tierra since 1980. Every week, they sell around 60 to 80 pounds of masa to Californios, the first Mexican restaurant in the world to win three Michelin stars. It might be the most crucial ingredient on the menu when you consider the rich nixtamalized corn dough used to make tortillas, tostadas, tamales, and chips has been at the core of Mesoamerican cuisine for centuries. Transcending sustenance, masa is instilled with a spirituality that goes back to Aztec creation myths detailing how humanity was formed from corn.

“These people are masters of their craft as farmers in this super-special growing region,” continues Cantú. “It just separates what we do — it’s that extra 1%.”

So, in June, a few days after the Michelin ceremony was held in San Diego, Cantú and the Californios crew showed up at the Ferry Plaza Farmers Market with a surprise thank-you card and bottle of wine for Lee and Wayne, who first met Cantú when he stumbled upon their stand in 2016.

The card read: “Thank you so much for sharing your amazing corn, beans, and chiles with us. You all are so inspiring to our team, and we are so thankful to share them with our guests.”

It’s been a long journey since the James family started selling grain corn dry on the cob in 2006. They later employed a thresher to remove it from the cob to sell as loose grain and eventually added three mills to make their own masa.

The main varieties of corn they grow include Mexican June, which is white, and the yellow Hickory King. Their blue-and-white Michoacán variety was started from seeds a worker brought back from his village in Mexico. But the most unique is their own Tierra Black corn that they painstakingly developed over the course of 10 years by breeding Peruvian purple corn with the multicolored Painted Mountain variety. It’s a lower yielding corn but is highly coveted by Cantú for its color and taste.

“Our guests are always asking us, ‘What’s in this masa or what’s in this tortilla?’” says Cantú, who loves the super-crispy black tostadas it makes. “We have to remind them that it’s just the masa — there are no other ingredients. Sometimes we’ll bring out the corn to show them.”

The far-flung origin stories behind many of the vegetables that Tierra sells to Californios would make a fascinating travelogue or book. The black turtle beans, procured from an Oregon farmer, unanimously passed a taste test among Tierra customers. Their red beans came from a family that dropped by the farmstand one day. “They said, ‘This is the bean we grow in Nicaragua. We really like it.’ So we started growing it, and it’s been great,” says Lee.

Other loyal customers brought back choricero and nora chiles from Spain. They got Espelette pepper seeds from chef and owner of San Francisco’s Zuni Café, Gilbert Pilgram, who also sources produce from the farm. Lee’s brother brought back a chilhuacle negro pepper from Oaxaca, and their chilhuacle amarillo came from chef Eric Tucker at Millennium, a venerable vegan restaurant in Oakland.

The Michelin stars come at a time when Tierra Vegetables is at a crossroads. For the past several years, Wayne and Lee James have mounted a fundraising campaign to buy the 10-acre farm from Sonoma County Agricultural Preservation and Open Space District, recently raising more than $100,000. But they’re now realizing it’s not feasible for them to own the property and they may use some of that donated money to continue farming and leasing it instead.

“The Ag and Open Space District, they don’t want us to leave, and they definitely don’t want to kick us off,” Lee says. “But they realize that we’re not going to be buying it, so now we have to figure out a lease.”

Over the years, Cantú has tried to help sustain the Windsor farm and its seven employees. When Tierra’s well gave out during Covid, he donated more than $10,000 to buy a new one. “He’s been very supportive of the farm financially,” says Lee.

Cantú is just happy to hear Tierra will continue farming. “I’m sure Wayne and Lee could make a whole lot more money growing grapes or whatever, but what they told me is that they like to grow food. They love growing things that are meant to be good for you.”

Unlike Tierra, which is laid out mostly in traditional farm rows, Stone Edge Farm unfolds in a patchwork of pocket gardens, what Eierman calls “shady corners and little nooks,” adding up to a 1-acre self-sustaining “micro-grid” farm on the 16-acre estate where Enclos co-owner Leslie McQuown lives. She and her late husband, Mac McQuown, founded Stone Edge Farm Estate Vineyards & Winery in 2004. They opened a dining room for club members in 2013 in an 1890s Victorian near Sonoma Plaza, which later became Edge restaurant. After major renovations, the space reopened as Enclos in 2024 and earned two Michelin stars its first year.

Eierman also tends fruit trees, garlic, winter squashes, and olives on an acre that’s part of the 120-acre Silver Cloud vineyard on Cavedale Road. And soon he will expand farming operations to Stone Edge Farm’s new La Maison tasting room property on Eighth Street East in Sonoma.

When the Montgomery High School graduate first teamed up with New Hampshire native Limoges in 2023, a full 18 months before Enclos opened its doors, they settled into a magical incubation period of brainstorming and dreaming up experimental dishes in a prep kitchen on the farm estate. “In the beginning we were just throwing everything at the wall,” remembers Limoges. “We would go through the seed book and just circle things that we thought looked cool.”

One of the first experiments was kumquats, a thimble-sized citrus that arrived in 15-gallon pots. Three years later, they’re almost ready for harvest but have yet to appear on the menu. After considering microgreens, they decided to focus on rare vegetables and fruits like habanadas, the magically heatless habanero pepper boasting zero Scoville units, and fraises des bois, known as Alpine strawberries.

Limoges sums up their mutual respect as “game recognizes game, iron sharpens iron.” Their mantra from the beginning was “let’s not force anything and make sure it feels good,” he says. “I think the restaurant really feeds off of the farm and vice versa, because it’s such a symbiotic relationship of what works well and utilizing what’s best for both entities.”

Every Tuesday and Friday Eierman drops off produce to the restaurant, trading it for the kitchen’s trim and scraps to turn into compost that will enrich the soil along with manure from a local dairy.

“Our organic philosophy is that if we build healthy soil that’s biologically active, we shouldn’t need to do much, and that’s going to give us the best flavors,” says Eierman. “A little bit of stress and a little bit of that plant fighting it out and finding nutrients in the soil can translate to a more flavorful product.”

In summer, Enclos serves a fresh heirloom tomato dish with at least 20 different varieties, some juiced and others turned into a gel. Accompanying it is a sheet of vellum listing the colorful heirloom names that each seem to have their own story to tell. Limoges describes how the staff adorns the window between the kitchen and dining room with a selection of different tomatoes. “When guests walk in, they’ll see that and subconsciously maybe something will click for them when they sit down, and they’ll want to have that dish,” he says.

Even with Eierman’s meticulous farming practices, Stone Edge is no stranger to the caprices of the harvest season. One of Enclos’ most visually arresting dishes, called Venison and Its Antlers, was inspired by Limoges’ meandering hikes in the Sonoma County backcountry as well as his home state of New Hampshire, where the deer is the state animal. It includes tender buds from a Grecian bay laurel tree at the farm that are salted, pickled, and pressure-cooked until they resemble capers. This past spring, thanks to an unseasonably warm March, bud break happened during a week when the restaurant was closed and the harvest window was so narrow that the buds opened before they could be picked.

“That was a tough call to make,” says Eierman, who now laughs about breaking the news to the chef. Fortunately they had preserved enough bay buds the previous year to last through another season.

While preserving those tiny buds may seem finicky, the goal is to transport guests to the farm through each fleeting microseason. “If there’s some way that we can talk about the growing season and how small of a window it is, and how beautiful it is, then I think that’s where the inspiration comes from.”

By now, as winter squash makes its way onto the menu in October, the glow of three Michelin stars has given way to the unspoken pressure to maintain the almost impossibly high level of service and cuisine another year. But Eierman and Limoges haven’t forgotten how they celebrated the day they heard the news: “We gave each other a big hug,” says Limoges. “And then we started talking about vegetables.”

Middleton Farm

Long before Troubadour won its first Michelin star in June, chef Sean McGaughey had forged his relationship with farmer Sam Calderon of Middleton Farm.

“Middleton was my introduction to Healdsburg farming,” says McGaughey, who worked at SingleThread when the two first met at the Healdsburg Farmers Market. “I would just point at a bunch of stuff, and then ask him to stop by the restaurant after the market, and I’d just take whatever off his hands,” remembers McGaughey, adding that the mulberries Calderon grew were so delicious, they would often just wash them and serve them in a cup with no other preparation. The produce was that good.

So, when he opened Troubadour Bread & Bistro in 2022 with his wife and co-owner Melissa McGaughey (the couple also owns Quail & Condor Bakery), he relied heavily on fresh produce from Middleton, along with produce from other local farms like Russian River Organics and Front Porch Farm.

Middleton Farm has been around for more than 60 years, most recently changing hands when it was bought in 2015 by San Francisco transplants Annie and Montgomery Woods. The one constant is Calderon, who has worked the 8 acres of rich alluvial soil near Mill Creek for more than 30 years.

“I’ve farmed all my life,” says Calderon, who learned to grow corn and avocados in the state of Michoacán in Mexico. “Since I am the oldest grandchild, I started working with my grandfather in the fields when I was 3 years old. It’s part of my life.”

When he was 14, Calderon immigrated to the U.S., laboring in Southern California citrus groves before heading north. After working with him for years, Annie Woods is starting to figure out his secret: “When you look at the product and the way it’s presented, you can tell that it was grown with a lot of love and care,” says Woods, who also supplies produce for nearly a dozen other Michelin-rated restaurants, including Cyrus, SingleThread, and Quince in San Francisco.

McGaughey agrees that Calderon has a magic touch. “It actually changes the way you cook,” he says of the soft-spoken farmer. “He lets the product speak for itself.”

title: Come for the Beer, Stay for the Pizza at Old Caz Backyard
summary:
Old Caz Backyard’s Petaluma kitchen goes beyond brewery food with slow-fermented pizzas that aren't afraid to get a little weird.

The post Come for the Beer, Stay for the Pizza at Old Caz Backyard appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The pepperoni pizza might lure you into Old Caz Backyard’s new kitchen, Caz Eats. But the Hot Pot pizza — topped with Sichuan peppercorns, maitake mushrooms, sausage, pickled chiles and kimchi — will keep you coming back.

Or so chef Elijah Trujillo hopes.

“I like ramen and hot pots, and this pizza just worked out,” he said.

There’s also a potato pizza with roasted leeks and potato chips, and the Pig N Pear, with pears, spicy sausage, chile crisp and crackly pork skin.

And yes, there are cheese, pepperoni and Margherita pizzas for traditionalists.

Trujillo and partner Kayla Hendrix are the duo behind the new Petaluma taproom’s menu. The two Shokakko food truck alums had little more than a month to create a menu of slow-fermented pizzas, big salads and wood-fired vegetables that elevate the average brewery menu.

Renovations kept them out of the kitchen until about three weeks before the launch.

“It takes time and effort to hone an outstanding pizza,” Trujillo said. Especially one that takes three days to ferment.

Time wasn’t on their side. Luckily, the pizza gods were.

The spot

Previously known as The Block, Old Caz took over the food truck park, beer garden and food program in August, celebrating its second location with a 7.3-mile, Olympic-torch-style procession. About 300 cyclists and 50 walkers made the trek from the brewery’s Rohnert Park taproom to the new Petaluma location, tap handle in tow, to pour the first beer.

Trujillo and Hendrix turned out dozens of pizzas for the hungry crowd, no small feat in a tiny kitchen mostly occupied by the oven. There’s no freezer and minimal refrigeration and pantry space, forcing the couple to rely on fresh ingredients and dough that ferments for three days.

The result is a chewy, blistered crust that can stand up to its toppings. Because Trujillo hates a floppy pizza.

Fresh vegetables and salads round out the menu, including some that might not always be fan favorites. Hendrix said one of her favorite reactions is hearing someone say they never liked beets before trying theirs.

“People feel like beets taste like dirt, and sometimes they do,” she said. “But there are so many things we can do with the great produce.”

Set on a cloud of tart yogurt and drizzled with pomegranate molasses and chile crisp, the beets make a side dish worthy of a standing ovation.

Cauliflower gets housemade garlic hummus, dukkah, pickled raisins and lemon. Sweet potatoes take a sweet-savory turn with salted maple syrup and vegan marshmallow.

The “Caesar is right here” salad made the menu after people immediately started asking where it was, given the Caesar’s seemingly mandatory place on every pizza menu.

Caz Eats is that kind of place — serious about pizza and happy to get a little weird.

Stay tuned for an even more extensive menu in spring 2027.

“There’s a lot more to come,” Hendrix said.

Best bets

Pizzas are shareable 12-inch pies, all notable for fresh ingredients and cheeses that include the usual mozzarella and Parmesan but venture into less-traveled territory with stracciatella, provolone and Bellwether Farms Carmody.

Hot Pot, $26: The pie built to keep you coming back, with Sichuan peppercorns, maitake mushrooms, sausage, pickled chiles and kimchi.

Cap N Stem, $26: A minimalist pie with maximal flavor, made with white sauce, Mycopia mushrooms, thyme, Carmody and lemon zest.

There’s a Leek, $24: White sauce, roasted leeks, shaved Yukon Gold potatoes, Carmody, crispy shallots and potato chips sprinkled on top.

Pig N Pear, $26: What started with roasted peaches has evolved with the season to include roasted pears, spicy sausage, chile crisp and crispy cracklings.

Salads, $14: The supersized Caesar and Local Greens, with local chicories and lettuces, shaved apples and pears, Point Reyes blue cheese and a sprinkle of seeds, are a welcome departure from the bagged iceberg-and-grated-carrot mix that makes me so sad.

Beet Salad, $14: I love beets, so this was an easy choice, made even easier by its puddle of yogurt, sweet pomegranate molasses and chile crisp. I’d eat this every day if I could. I’m not going to say everyone will love it, but I challenge you to hate it.

Local food trucks and tents are almost always on hand, including my smashburger favorite, Thanks for the Invite.

Caz Eats is open 3-8 p.m. Monday through Friday and 1-8 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. Old Caz Backyard is at 20 Grey St., Petaluma; 707-347-5932, oldcaz.com/backyard.

title: There Are Never Enough Lemons at Spread Kitchen in Sonoma
summary:
Chef Cristina Topham brings Lebanese-inspired cooking, local produce and plenty of lemon, garlic and spice to Spread Kitchen in Sonoma.

The post There Are Never Enough Lemons at Spread Kitchen in Sonoma appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Lemons, garlic and olive oil are the backbone of Cristina Topham’s cooking at Spread Kitchen in Sonoma. The chef-owner goes through roughly 680 lemons a week at her Lebanese-inspired restaurant in Boyes Hot Springs, squeezing citrus into everything from hummus and salads to marinades and sauces.

And somehow, she still finds herself saying the same thing.

“It needs more lemon.”

Big flavors are the point at Spread Kitchen. Topham leans on fresh herbs and spices, including za’atar from Lebanon, sheep’s-milk feta from Bulgaria and as much as 50 pounds of garlic a week.

“I’m here every day with spoons, tasting everything because I want it to be consistent,” she said.

A third-generation Lebanese American, she also gets plenty of advice from family, including her mother, who offered a familiar suggestion for the tabbouleh when the restaurant opened in 2022: more lemon.

Topham opened Spread Kitchen after years as a caterer, private chef and restaurant cook. She had worked in Paris, cooked in private homes and aboard yachts, and later used a $20,000 win on the first season of Guy Fieri’s “Guy’s Grocery Games” to launch her catering business.

It wasn’t until she was 50, though, that she made the leap to her own brick-and-mortar restaurant. She learned Spanish to communicate with her staff, taught herself bookkeeping and picked up a few hard lessons about overhiring along the way.

The menu was an easier lift, evolving naturally from her Lebanese roots. Topham is obsessive about using ingredients from local farms, letting the seasons dictate what appears on the plate: melons, tomatoes, Jimmy Nardello peppers and figs in late summer; Brussels sprouts only in winter. Sometimes, to her customers’ consternation, favorites disappear when their season ends.

“If people saw the quality of produce in and out of season, they’d be so surprised. It’s a really big difference,” she said.

That’s why everything has its moment in Topham’s kitchen, changing and evolving throughout the year with what’s at its peak.

Except lemon. There’s always room for more lemon.

Best bets

Dip plates: You can order as many of the cold mezze dips as you want, but go for all five ($26), just because you can — and because they’re worth it. The creamy Lebanese hummus is the standard-bearer, topped with black chickpeas from Rancho Gordo. Baba ghanoush is smoky without bitterness, with just a hint of char. Red pepper muhammara gets a sweet lift from pomegranate syrup, while beet and whipped feta and light labneh with preserved lemons round out the lineup. Served with warm pita.

Seasonal salad, $10: There’s no wrong season for Topham’s salad of the moment, but the current version — local heirloom melons with Urfa chile, feta, pistachios and sumac — is so good you’ll wish melon season lasted all year. Fattoush salad ($16) is a menu regular, with creamy pomegranate vinaigrette and mint.

Dirty fries, $14: A pile of thin, crisp fries gets the star treatment with feta, za’atar, tahini-yogurt dressing and pickled onions. Stupid good.

Grain bowl: Topham’s cooking is best experienced in a heaping bowl of saffron rice studded with apricots and topped with meaty lamb kofta, drizzled with tahini-yogurt sauce. It comes with hummus, well-seasoned quinoa tabbouleh (it’s the lemon), pickled vegetables and pita. Fried cauliflower or falafel with green tahini are excellent vegetarian options.

Chicken lavash wrap, $18; small, $12: Thin lavash wraps around turmeric-infused chicken loaded with cabbage, pickled onions, pickled cucumbers and herbs. A generous slather of creamy toum pulls it all together. The vegetarian falafel version is equally good. Make it “Local Style,” with hummus and hot sauce inside, for $2 more.

Mahalabia, $7: This creamy milk pudding is perfumed with cardamom and cinnamon and topped with seasonal fruit, currently figs. Ground arborio rice thickens the vegan dessert, made with coconut and oat milk.

Drinks: Beer, hard cider and wine are available by the glass or bottle. Orange-blossom lemonade and minty Lebanese tea ($4.50 each) are especially good with the food. Local juices, kombucha, CBD-infused drinks and gourmet sodas round out the menu.

Cold case: Don’t miss the toum, a creamy whipped garlic sauce that’s irresistible on za’atar fries — and conveniently available to take home.

Many gluten-free, vegetarian and vegan options are available.

The vibe: The quiet, dog-friendly patio is an urban oasis. Park yourself under a shady tree or one of the big umbrellas for a relaxing afternoon of dipping and sipping. Inside, the tiny Boyes Hot Springs cafe has a neighborhood feel, usually filled with locals grabbing lunch and gossiping over warm pita.

Fun fact: While cooking aboard a yacht, Topham spent four days battling 40-foot waves in the Bermuda Triangle. At one point, the boom crashed through the pilothouse just feet from where she was standing.

The spot: Spread Kitchen is open from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. 18375 Highway 12, Sonoma; 707-721-1256; spreadkitchensonoma.com

title: Top Sonoma County Spots for Your Morning Coffee
summary:
Here are our go-to coffee shops and cafes in Sonoma County for a great cup of joe every day.

The post Top Sonoma County Spots for Your Morning Coffee appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County may be known for its wine and beer, but the same devotion to craft brewing applies to coffee. Here are some of our favorite coffee shops in the area, from longtime local institutions to newer spots worth seeking out.

Santa Rosa

A’Roma Roasters

The brick-walled coffee shop in Railroad Square draws college students and artsy locals who come for the coffee and often stay late for live music. Choose from a selection of fresh roasts, including the signature Iced A’Roma coffee with vanilla, or try a silky cappuccino with a coconut macaroon. 95 Fifth St., Santa Rosa, 707-576-7765, aromaroasters.com

Blue Bottle Coffee

The Santa Rosa outpost of the Oakland-based coffee company emphasizes single-origin beans and carefully calibrated brewing methods over heavily flavored drinks. 701 Village Court at Montgomery Village, Suite D5, Santa Rosa, bluebottlecoffee.com

Brew

There’s more to Brew than a regular cup of coffee. With rotating herbal-inspired lattes, craft beer and an open, welcoming atmosphere, it’s a good place to spend a sunny afternoon on the patio, whether you’re reading or, as we sometimes do, conducting an interview. 555 Healdsburg Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-303-7372, brewcoffeeandbeer.com 

Café des Croissants

Pair your coffee with something from the breakfast or lunch menu, such as the Normandy egg sandwich with sausage and cheese or the chicken salad sandwich served on a croissant. 990 Sonoma Ave., Suite 1, Santa Rosa, 707-308-4243; 2444 Lomitas Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-544-6710, cafedescroissants.com

Crooks Coffee

Crooks is known for its creme brûlée lattes and wide selection of pastries, along with an airy, modern interior. 404 Mendocino Ave., Suite C, Santa Rosa, 707-791-3365, crookscoffeehouse.com

Land and Water Coffee

This Santa Rosa coffee shop has a following for its premium roasts and breakfast offerings. Try the vanilla latte year-round or, in fall, the pumpkin spice latte, with its cinnamon sweetness. The menu also includes avocado toast and baked goods from Sarmentine artisan bakery. 621 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-527-3731; 1301 Cleveland Ave., Suite B, Santa Rosa, 707-527-3725, landandwater.coffee

Little Deer

Formerly Cafe Frida, this SOFA district cafe offers simple bites including breakfast burritos, salads, croissants and scones, along with espresso and tea. 300 South A St., Santa Rosa, 707-308-4344, cafelittledeer.com

Redwood Gospel Bakery & Cafe

Faith isn’t a prerequisite for stopping in for coffee and pastries at Redwood Gospel Mission Baking Co., which opened in mid-April. The coffeehouse and bakery serves housemade croissants, scones, sandwiches, salads and espresso drinks. 2447 Summerfield Road, Santa Rosa, rgm.org

Rollup

The cyclist-oriented cafe serves espresso drinks, drip coffee, matcha and chai. Revolution Bread provides hearty toast options and weekly sweet treats. 121 Fifth St., Santa Rosa, 707-888-1924, rolluptocoffee.com

SoCo Coffee

Part coffee shop, part taco bar, SoCo Coffee is a place to get both an espresso and a breakfast burrito. The shop also has a large collection of books to browse — just be careful with the taco drippings. 1015 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-527-6434, instagram.com/sococoffeeco

Kenwood

Pillowfight Coffee

Named after Kenwood’s historic World Pillow Fighting Championships, Pillowfight Coffee serves locally sourced coffee, tea, matcha and food. Try a latte with a seasonal syrup, such as the pumpkin, along with a pastry or slice of vegetable quiche. 8910 Sonoma Highway, Suite B12, Kenwood, pillowfight.coffee

Sonoma

Café Scooteria

If you need a caffeine fix while your motorcycle is being serviced, Café Scooteria may be the place. Next to Sonoma’s Wingo Motorcycles, the drive-through cafe pairs coffee with retro vehicles and is built around a 1966 Lambretta three-wheeled scooter. Pair an espresso with a croissant before heading down the road. 455 W. Napa St., Sonoma, 707-938-0800, instagram.com/cafescooteria

Smastad Coffee Roasters

Formerly Barking Dog Roasters, this Swedish-inspired cafe is a no-frills spot that has been roasting coffee beans to its own specifications for nearly 30 years. Locals flock to the funky mainstay for its coffee. For a cozy afternoon, try a classic cappuccino with a housemade pear-cinnamon muffin. 981 Broadway, Sonoma, 707-939-1906, smastadcoffee.com

Sunflower Caffe

On Sonoma’s historic square, this Wine Country brunch staple is not what you’d typically call a coffee shop. But its prime people-watching location and good coffee earn it a place here. Come for the extensive brunch menu and chai lattes; stay for the location. 421 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-6645, sonomasunflower.com

Petaluma

Caffeine Inc.

This coffee shop near the Petaluma Marina serves coffee and light bites in a laid-back setting with views of the water. Try a seasonal latte with avocado toast or a morning pastry. There is also a matcha bar with options such as strawberry matcha and iced matcha Americano. 775 Baywood Drive, Petaluma, 707-774-6016, caffeineinc.net

Della Fattoria

The chai and honey-lavender lattes are worth ordering, as are the baked goods. Start with a bear claw, chocolate croissant, focaccia or fruit galette. For a more substantial meal, there are pancakes, breakfast scrambles, eggs Benedict, salads and sandwiches. 143 Petaluma Blvd. N., Petaluma, 707-763-0161, dellafattoria.com

Grand Central Petaluma

Family-owned Grand Central Petaluma sources coffee beans from co-owner Juan Carlos’ native Ecuador and serves locally sourced, South American-style empanadas. Popular drinks include the horchata latte and a rotating featured mocha, currently pistachio-flavored, made with hand-mixed chocolate. 226 Weller St., Petaluma, 707-774-6131, grandcentralpetaluma.com

Petaluma Coffee & Tea Co.

Founded as Petaluma Coffee Company in 1989, the business added tea in 1998. Founders Gardner and Sheila Bride have been serving coffee for more than 30 years. Sip a simple but robust cup of coffee or try a more elaborate drink such as the London Smog, made with espresso, chocolate powder, Earl Grey-infused syrup and a bergamot-peel garnish. 212 Second St., Petaluma, 707-763-2727, petalumacoffee.com

Cotati

Cotati Coffee Company

Full of local charm, Cotati Coffee Company serves creative caffeinated drinks and locally sourced pastries. Try the Almond Roca Mocha, inspired by the nutty chocolate candy. Coffee comes in a quirky “T-Rexacorn” cup — part Tyrannosaurus rex, part unicorn — and drinks may arrive with foam art depicting bears, dragons and other creatures. 8225 Old Redwood Highway, Cotati, 707-992-0005, cotati-coffee-company.square.site

Rohnert Park

Sandpino’s Coffee & Brews

This all-day coffee shop serves coffee and matcha drinks alongside Salvadoran and Mexican food. 101 Golf Course Drive, Suite A3, Rohnert Park, instagram.com/sandpinoscoffeeandbrews

Graton

Graton Station

This weekend coffee cart outside the former Graton firehouse serves a simple menu of coffee, tea and pastries. Plans to expand into a full cafe and bakery include a larger breakfast and lunch menu with toasts, soups, salads and sandwiches. 3120 Ross Road, Sebastopol, instagram.com/gratonstation

Sebastopol

Retrograde Coffee Roasters

This Sebastopol outpost is a mainstay for west county locals who favor the Rocket Man cold brew, housemade hemp-coconut milk and specialty lattes. Matcha and turmeric drinks are also perennial favorites. The small-batch bean roastery began as a pop-up at an Oakland bagel shop in 2014 before moving north to Sonoma County and opening its brick-and-mortar location in downtown Sebastopol. 130 South Main St., Suite 103, Sebastopol, 707-827-8065, retrograderoasters.com

Taylor Lane Organic Coffee

Taylor Lane’s origin story is one of the more distinctly West County tales of local business. The roasting operation began in 1993 inside an old barn on a 100-acre farm on Occidental’s Taylor Lane. Formerly Taylor Maid, the Sebastopol shop is a destination for coffee drinkers. Try the lavender latte, a classic cappuccino or a drink made with housemade pumpkin syrup. 6790 McKinley St., Suite 170, Sebastopol, taylorlane.com

Wylde Playground & Café

This kid-friendly, health-conscious playground and cafe is a collaboration between the owners of Terrapin Creek restaurant in Bodega Bay and The Barn Fitness Collective. The menu includes coffee, kombucha, beer, hard cider and grab-and-go protein bowls. 500 Robinson Road, Sebastopol, Instagram.com/wyldeplaygroundcafe

Windsor

Grey Squirrel Manor

This woodland-inspired cafe takes its name and character from a vest-wearing squirrel mascot. The menu includes creative matchas, lattes and other drinks, with an option to add sweet, fluffy cold foam. 630 McClelland Drive, Windsor, 707-243-3551, greysquirrelmanor.com

Healdsburg

Black Oak Coffee Roasters

Black Oak Coffee Roasters serves coffee in a chic, minimalist setting. For something sweet, try the Lovers Lane Latte, made with local wildflower honey and bee pollen, or the Lavender Latte with housemade lavender syrup and an organic lavender garnish. 324 Center St., Healdsburg, 866-390-1427, blackoakcoffee.com

Flying Goat Coffee

The coffee at Flying Goat is good, but what to order? Try the Aztec Mocha, made with double espresso, Valrhona chocolate, chilies, spices, vanilla, organic cane sugar, rose water and steamed milk. 419 Center St. and 300 Center St., Healdsburg, flyinggoatcoffee.com

Quail & Condor

The bakery serves freshly brewed medium-roast coffee from Black Oak Coffee Roasters alongside pastries including croissants and oatmeal cream pies. 44 Mill St., Unit J, Healdsburg, 707-473-8254, quailandcondor.com

Sonoma Coast

Cafe Aquatica

It would be hard to find a Sonoma County coffee shop with a better view than Jenner’s Cafe Aquatica. At the mouth of the Russian River, the aquatic-themed coffee shop has a large outdoor seating area where patrons can sip coffee just feet from the water. The menu includes plenty of vegetarian and vegan options. 10439 Highway 1, Jenner, 707-865-2251, cafeaquatica.com

Gold Coast Coffee & Bakery

A favorite stop on the way to the coast, Gold Coast serves coffee and housemade pastries on a deck surrounded by greenery. Try the Cafe Cubano or an iced mocha, followed by a cinnamon roll or bear claw. 25377 Steelhead Blvd., Duncans Mills, 707-865-1441, goldcoastcoffeebakery.com

Roadhouse Coffee

This cafe near Bodega Harbor is filled with books, local artwork and stringed instruments, giving it a particularly cozy feel. Order the cinnamon-spiced Mexican Mocha, a local favorite, with blueberry coffee cake. 1580 Eastshore Road, Bodega Bay, 707-360-8856

Multiple locations

Avid Coffee

Formerly Acre Coffee, this local chain changed its name and ownership in 2021. Owner Rob Daly has spent much of his career in the coffee business, working at Wolf Coffee and Starbucks before serving as CEO of Taylor Lane Organic Coffee. Expect espresso and other coffee drinks. 21 Fourth St., Petaluma, 707-772-5117; 2365 Midway Drive, Santa Rosa, 707-595-5984, avidcoffee.com

BoCo Coffee

This Vietnamese coffee pop-up is a favorite at the Saturday farmers market at Luther Burbank Center for the Arts. Its signature egg coffee, or cà phê trứng, combines whipped egg yolk, sugar and condensed milk into custard-like foam over strong Vietnamese coffee. Seasonal teas and matchas are also available. Pop-up schedule at instagram.com/drink_boco.

Plank Coffee

This trendy cafe serves coffee, breakfast bites, vegan options and milk alternatives. A popular choice is the Cinnabang, made with house-roasted espresso, sweetened condensed milk and cinnamon. 175 Dry Creek Road, Healdsburg, 707-395-0572; 227 N. Cloverdale Blvd., Cloverdale, 707-894-6187, plankcoffee.com

Sunshine Coffee Roasters

Sunshine Coffee Roasters has been roasting small-batch organic coffee since 2004 and now operates two retail locations. Regulars praise its specialty horchata lattes and friendly baristas. If elaborate espresso drinks aren’t your thing, try the cold brew. 6656 Front St., Forestville, 707-887-1632; 1691 Highway 116 N., Sebastopol, 707-823-2664, sunshinecoffeeroasters.com

Heather Irwin, Maci Martell and Christi Warren contributed to this article.

title: ‘She Gives So Much’: Quivira Vineyards’ Ancient Fig Tree Continues To Provide
summary:
As the matriarch of Quivira Vineyards’ 100-plus acres, the ancient fig tree is a treasure trove of fruit and history.

The post ‘She Gives So Much’: Quivira Vineyards’ Ancient Fig Tree Continues To Provide appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Long before grapes were the dominant crop in Healdsburg’s Dry Creek Valley, the farmers in this fertile stretch of land grew wheat and hay. On their homesteads they raised cattle and pigs, cultivated gardens, and planted orchards with all varieties of fruit. In 1876, amid America’s centennial celebrations, a fig sapling sprang from the earth on a parcel of land near the banks of Dry Creek, a determined botanical specimen that has continued to serve forth its fruit for 150 years.

Now the matriarch of Quivira Vineyards’ 100-plus acres, the tree is feted each year with a dinner that culminates with diners riding a tram through the vineyards along a tributary to Dry Creek to a spot where the vines make way for the guest of honor, which is festooned with twinkling lights. There, they raise a toast with Quivira’s Fig Tree Sauvignon Blanc paired with fig and fresh berry tartlets.

The tree’s presence is so integral to this property, it’s taken on a personality. Quivira’s general manager, Steve Domenichelli, refers to it as “the old gal.” Perhaps at one time she was tall and stately, but today she’s a bit stooped, held together with chains due to injuries suffered in a lightning strike. Still, she continues to provide.

“The fruit is really rich, beautiful and luscious. It just gets better with time,” says Quivira’s chef, Julia Gnall, noting the tree is so big that birds get the fruit that’s out of reach. But it still gives her plenty to work with.

For the birthday dinner, Gnall prepared roasted-fig salad with whipped feta dressed in fig vinaigrette. What figs don’t get used for winery dinners, Gnall freezes for making purees or fig upside-down cakes. She also plans to make about 80 jars of spicy fig jam to serve in the fall and winter months with cheese plates, or perhaps in a warm puff pastry-wrapped brie appetizer.

Gnall sees it as her duty to preserve the fruit from the formidable tree, along with the bounty of produce grown on Quivira’s organic farm.

“I want to honor and respect it,” she says. “I see how hard Mother Nature works changing and growing and going from something that every year has to start over, even though trapped inside of it is millennia of knowledge and history.”

One of Gnall’s earliest childhood memories is of plucking figs at her aunt’s home in Southern California and sticking her thumb into their plump bottoms to get to the sweet, tender flesh inside. Working with figs from Quivira’s ancient tree brings back those taste memories, and like Domenichelli, the chef feels the tree has seen and prevailed over so much history in this valley that its spirit can be felt.

“She gives so much. It feels like the old gal is beckoning you in. ‘Come sit in my shade, eat my fruit, and I’ll tell you stories.'” says Gnall. “It’s like ‘The Giving Tree.’ She’s just so happy to be there.”

Roasted Fig Vinaigrette

Makes 2 cups

Quivira Vineyards chef Julia Gnall roasts figs that serve a dual purpose. She uses some in a salad with fresh lettuce, pickled onions, feta and pumpkin seeds. The rest get pureed for a dressing that’s drizzled over all of it.

  • 2 tbsp. roasted fig puree
  • 1 tbsp. Dijon mustard
  • 1 tsp. fresh thyme
  • 1 garlic clove, grated or minced
  • 1/4 cup balsamic vinegar
  • 1 tsp. kosher salt
  • Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
  • 1 cup good-quality olive oil, plus more for drizzling

First, make the fig puree. Preheat oven to 425 degrees. Wash and trim the tops off of 12-15 figs, then slice in half lengthwise. Place figs halves face-up on a parchment-lined sheet pan, drizzle with olive oil, and season with salt and pepper. Roast figs for 15 minutes then allow to cool. Reserve 12-18 halves to use in the salad. Place 12 fig halves in a blender or food processor and puree. Remove all but 2 tablespoons of the puree and refrigerate or freeze for another use. Add mustard, thyme, garlic, balsamic vinegar, salt, and pepper to the processor along with the puree and blend until well combined. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil and process until the mixture is emulsified.

title: The Redmetal Barn Art Gallery Might Be Cloverdale’s Best-Kept Secret
summary:
A nearly century-old farmhouse and two aging horse barns in rural Cloverdale have been restored as a home and eclectic art galleries.

The post The Redmetal Barn Art Gallery Might Be Cloverdale’s Best-Kept Secret appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
The couple wasn’t sure they were in the right place. They had followed directions to an unkempt vineyard outside Cloverdale, where, on a sweltering July afternoon, the dusty parking lot looked more suited to farm equipment than fine art. They rolled down the window and asked whether the gallery was really open to the public. It was — and they soon joined several dozen others making their way across River Road to the Redmetal Barn.

A short drive from the historic Asti Winery by way of Cloverdale’s seasonal summer bridge, the secluded gallery has hosted quarterly exhibitions, known mostly by word of mouth, for nearly a decade. Its curator is Cloverdale resident Jenness Brewer, a retired television advertising executive whose goals upon retiring nearly 20 years ago were simple: “Be outside, go for walks, look at art.”

In 2013, she found the ideal place to do just that: a small property along River Road with a nearly century-old farmhouse and two aging horse barns. Brewer recalls that within minutes of stepping inside the two-story farmhouse, she told the Realtor she would take it, before even seeing the kitchen or living room. The daughter of a Connecticut tobacco farmer, the rural setting was reminiscent of the small town where Brewer grew up, right down to the river running through it. “It reminded me so much of Connecticut, and I thought my father would be so proud of me,” she says.

Brewer spent nearly a year renovating the property but left the home’s character largely intact. That included preserving a stone fireplace in the living room built by an uncle of the original owners, the Giannecchini family. A wall separating the living room from the spacious farmhouse-style kitchen was replaced with open shelving, creating an airier first floor while adding storage for dishware. The dining room, anchored by a long wooden table with ample space for lively family meals, doubles as an art gallery lined with paintings and found-object sculpture. Everywhere you look, there are curios and artworks that reveal Brewer’s keen eye for craftsmanship and understated sense of whimsy.

Upstairs are four bedrooms; three are reserved for visits from her grown daughters. The fourth, hidden behind a bookcase, is a secret room she had designed as a drawing room for her late partner. Here, the wood floors and window and door frames retain the rich stain they would have had a century ago. One bedroom is covered in wallpaper featuring barns that Brewer believes is original to the house.

Every day, Brewer climbs a hill overlooking the property using a curving railroad-tie staircase with exactly 73 steps, installed seven years ago, serendipitously, during her 73rd year. “It’s just a coincidence. It was not planned at all,” she says.

At the top, she settles into a chair and looks out over the barns, the olive grove she had planted, and, beyond it, the treeline along the Russian River. “We tend to go up there most every evening and just sit and look at how beautiful the vineyard is across from us,” she says. “It’s so calming and lovely and beautiful. In the full moon you can see the outline of the hills.”

When Brewer moved in, there were two barns. One, a dilapidated structure with a failing foundation, sat at the base of a hill and seemed determined to slide toward the Russian River. She wrestled with trying to save it, but practicality, along with a desire for gallery and studio space, ultimately prevailed. The red metal barn was born.

Brewer worked with Seattle-based architect Andrew Borges and Sebastopol builder Richard Hart — collaborators on her home renovation — to build a barn that reflects its rural setting while creating a modern space suited for fine art. Santa Rosa-based SC Barns fabricated the exterior. The interior is a blank slate, always ready to showcase each fleeting exhibition. The wall studs were installed specifically to support large-scale works, and gallery lighting runs the length of the lofted ceiling. One studio is used by Los Angeles-based artist Michael Deyermond; another houses equipment for the grove of 100 olive trees, which will be ready for harvest at the end of October.

The mossy patina on the second barn hints at its age. A date scratched into a board near the door — July 8, 1917 — offers a substantial clue. According to Brewer, it’s the oldest barn in Cloverdale and was moved onto the property from elsewhere in town early in the last century. It, too, needed restoring, so Brewer enlisted Nick Rupiper, a former River Road neighbor who now lives in Sonoma. He had previously built a bridge over the property’s seasonal stream, along with the tables used at every event. “He spent four or five months in there trying to figure it out,” Brewer says.

She calls it the owl barn, after the wise but elusive denizen that has taken up residence in its rafters. She has never seen it, but her 5-year-old grandson has. The bird leaves unmistakable evidence of its presence. “I see his droppings every day,” Brewer says with some amusement. “Just before every show I have the floor power washed.”

During the quarterly exhibits, the owl barn serves as an annex for an eclectic mix of rotating work: giant woodblock prints by Oakland artist Sandy Walker; found objects woven into fantastical installations by Los Angeles-based artist Nancy Kyes; and pieces by local artists Brooke Bannister and M.E. Moore that reflect a reverence for the natural world along the banks and beds of the Russian River. The only rule for exhibiting at Redmetal Barn, Brewer says, is that it has to be work she likes.

Brewer grew up “surrounded by art,” attending the Art Students League of New York before studying at the now-closed Burnley School of Design in Seattle. She found the prospect of making a living as an artist daunting and was twice married to professional artists, making it especially gratifying to provide a venue to showcase artists’ work. “I wanted to have other people be exposed to work that I found to be important and I wanted to see new work also,” she says. “I know how difficult it is for artists to get exposure and make a living.”

She takes no commission on sales, preferring to think of Redmetal Barn as an “unofficial nonprofit.” She also makes a point of including artwork at a range of price points, so visitors can find something within reach.

Between the fall and winter exhibitions comes Brewer’s favorite time on the farm: olive harvest. Two of her daughters fly in from Copenhagen and Atlanta to join a third, who lives in Cloverdale with her family. The gathering coincides with a host of family birthdays, and on the last Sunday in October, they typically rise before dawn, share a hearty breakfast in the owl barn, then spend the morning harvesting olives under the direction of Stuart Fisher, who tends the trees. “It’s grueling work,” Brewer says, but any discomfort is eclipsed by the camaraderie. “People are talking. It’s a wonderful, very festive morning.”

They break for lunch — salad, pasta and dessert prepared by Brewer’s daughters, Cleo and Nina — then return to the harvest if needed. Fisher loads the olives into his truck and drives them to Hopland, where they are pressed that same afternoon.

On a property restored to celebrate beauty and foster connection, Brewer says, “It’s really centered around family more than anything else.” But four days each year, Redmetal Barn extends that sense of connection to the broader community.

“It doesn’t feel like a gallery; it feels much more community-based,” says Brewer’s friend Marne Dupere, a Cloverdale business owner who guest-curated an exhibition earlier this year. “Once people go, they have this moment of surprise that’s really lovely. It does feel like a little secret — that you’ve been invited to this after-party that nobody knew about.”

While many, like Dupere, see the ways Cloverdale has benefited from everything Brewer has poured into Redmetal Barn, Brewer believes she’s the fortunate one.

“This is a unique community,” she says. “There’s a lot of support from everyone. I just feel so lucky that this was the community that I found.”

title: SlowDigz Founder Creates Eco-Fashion From Her Flourishing Sebastopol Microgarden
summary:
Lisa Rogers's bountiful home garden feeds her unique floral art business, where she creates one-of-a-kind, farm-to-fabric garments and textiles.

The post SlowDigz Founder Creates Eco-Fashion From Her Flourishing Sebastopol Microgarden appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
As late summer eases into early fall and many a flower garden is nodding off, Lisa Rogers’ little landscape is still rocking. The front yard of her home in a single-lane subdivision in Sebastopol looks like the final curtain call of the gardening season with the cast of crowd pleasers, from marigolds and sunflowers to goldenrod and black-eyed Susans, packed leaf-to-petal for a resounding final bow. For Rogers, this spectacle offers more than curb appeal. Her 3,000-square-foot city lot is a micro farm, and this is peak harvest when she gathers fresh leaves and flowers to dry, press, or process into natural dyes and botanical prints.

In late 2020, after years of experimentation and perfecting the art of botanical dyeing and printing — creating images on fabrics using flowers and leaves — she launched SlowDigz Eco Designs to market her handcrafted clothing and household textiles and teach the process to others. “I’m obsessed with trees and nature. I got arrested for trees,” she confesses of the time she took a break from biology studies at UC Santa Cruz to join logging protests on the North Coast in the 1990s. “I have a lot of passion for conservation and being outside.”

Now her conservation work is centered around saving seeds and preserving her garden for her one-of-a-kind, farm-to-fabric scarves, bandanas, tea towels, eye pillows, clothing, socks and more. At a time when AI-generated textiles and designs are showing up in stores, Rogers is patiently producing slow fashion from her garden and garage.

Ecoprinting involves steaming or boiling bundles of plant materials to transfer their colors and patterns onto natural fabrics like linen and wool. What emerges is rarely predictable and leads to inimitable colors and images that may be shockingly bold or softly ethereal and impressionistic.

“It came out such a beautiful shade of red!” Rogers gasps as she opens a Ball jar to pull out a test swatch of silken linen that has been marinating in a solution mixed with the roots of dyer’s madder (Rubia tinctorum), an herbaceous perennial. Rogers grows hers in a raised bed because it can quickly become invasive. She thrills to this magical element of the process. “I find so much joy teaching others botanical printing,” she says. “I love seeing their faces light up when they unwrap a bundle.”

To serve her craftmaking, Rogers maximized space to grow an extraordinary array of plants. While the main garden takes over the front yard, more plants flourish in pots along the side yard and in the back where her husband, Nieko, a builder who supervises residential construction projects, managed to carve out a covered corner oasis for chilling out.

Most of Rogers’ plants are functional, either to feed her unique floral art business or her family; tomatoes, potatoes and herbs are strategically tucked in among the flowers. Amid the striking coreopsis and cosmos that are key ingredients for her dyes and printing, are tropicals such as a bird of paradise and a banana tree that has yet to fruit, nostalgic reminders of Nieko’s native Hawaii and their time living on the north end of Oahu. She uses taro leaves for printing and loves experimenting with new plants like hardy hibiscus and passion fruit.

“I’m always trying to find new plants that will fit in my tiny garden,” she says, chuckling at the absurdity of squeezing in anything more, which she always manages to do. Clever with space, she carved a compact studio into the end of her single car garage. Here she stores materials and prepares the fabric, first by scouring to remove any impurities, waxes and oils. Then she soaks them overnight in a big pot of boiling water mixed with a mordant, such as alum, which allows the fabric to bond with dye.

For printing, she arranges flowers or leaves onto the prepared fabric and rolls it up on a dowel, often with a parchment barrier to prevent “ghost images.” After that she steams or simmers them in a dye bath. She also practices and teaches tataki zome, an easier form of ecoprinting, by pounding flowers onto paper or fabric.

She discovered ecoprinting 15 years ago at a workshop at San Francisco’s Exploratorium taught by India Flint, a self-described “botanical alchemist” from Australia who is credited with creating the artform.

“She showed us how to ecoprint with leaves and I had goosebumps and was really blown away,” Rogers says. “I had no idea she was the mother of ecoprinting, but I knew I wanted more of this in my life someday.”

The opportunity arose during the Covid pandemic when she explored natural dyes more deeply through online classes. “I began making indigo vats and started growing a small dye garden and attempting flower printing. I’ve had several fails over the years,” she says, “but kept planting and experimenting.”

Rogers moved here in 2019 after many years in Lake County, where she taught middle school science and later oversaw school garden programs, fulfilling her desire to be outdoors. She and Nieko looked high and low in Sonoma County for an affordable rural property suitable for gardening but couldn’t find anything within their budget, so they settled on a smaller place close to town and set about making the most of the space they have.

Using the lasagna method, the couple laid a cardboard carpet in the yard to kill weeds and topped it with layers of compost, leaves, manure and straw to build a rich soil. Their garden at first contained more food crops, but with so much fresh produce readily available in Sonoma County, Rogers found herself devoting more space to plants that lend themselves to printing or dyeing.

Among her favorites are dyer’s chamomile, little pops of sunshine with greenish-blue leaves; ‘Bright Lights’ cosmos, petite annuals with orange petals and rays of yellow shooting from their centers; and ‘Black Knight’ scabiosa, a pincushion flower with dramatic deep burgundy blooms that appear almost black perched on tall, thin stems.

As someone who has always felt bound to nature — her happy place growing up in Sunnyvale was spending birthdays at the beach and summers at her grandparents’ lakeside cottage in New Hampshire — she loves the idea of wearing natural fibers colored by plants. “It’s really neat to walk out into the forest and know I’m wearing leaf prints from that black walnut tree or from that eucalyptus,” she says. “It’s like a living piece.”

When Rogers’ garden reaches its peak in late summer and early fall, she takes advantage of the bounty by holding workshops in the North Bay. Whatever she can’t get out of her own garden she sources from a few local florists and farmers. She scours thrift shops for used clothing and fabrics made of linen, cotton, silk or wool, and sources new materials at places like Dharma Trading Co. in San Rafael, where she also teaches classes.

In addition to her eco arts, Rogers works as a senior park aide at Sonoma Coast State Park, where she gets to hang out in a kiosk near the crashing waves and greet beachgoers from all over. She finds the two jobs are a perfect balance of being in — and working from — the natural world. “I love walking by the ocean, amongst trees and flowers in forests and gardens,” she says. “Connecting others to nature through both of my jobs is where I’m meant to be.”
